q: Who ranks the work in the backlog, and on what basis?
options: The scrum master, by technical difficulty
The product owner, by business value
The development team, by personal preference
explanation: The product owner is responsible for guiding the direction of the product and ranks the work based on its business value.

q: What does MoSCoW stand for?
options: Major, optional, standard, critical, wanted items
Must have, should have, could have, will not have
explanation: MoSCoW sorts items into must have, should have, could have and will not have. It is fast for workshops but coarse and subjective.

q: A release is running short of time. Using MoSCoW, which items should be dropped first?
explanation: Could-have items are nice to have and are the first to go. Must-have items are essential to the release and are never dropped.

q: Customers of a banking app take it for granted that they can see their balance. They would be upset if it were missing, yet having it does not delight anyone. In Kano analysis, which type of feature is this?
explanation: Kano classifies features as basic, performance or delighter. A basic feature is taken for granted; only its absence is noticed.

q: A hotel surprises a guest with a free room upgrade. In Kano terms, what kind of feature is this?
explanation: A delighter is unexpected. Its presence pleases the customer and its absence is not missed.

q: How is weighted shortest job first (WSJF) calculated?
options: Job size divided by cost of delay
Cost of delay multiplied by job size
Cost of delay divided by job size
explanation: WSJF ranks work by dividing its cost of delay by its job size, favoring items that deliver the highest value in the shortest time.
ref: Agile Practice Guide, Glossary (weighted shortest job first)

links.label: Agile Practice Guide, Glossary (weighted shortest job first)

q: Item A has a cost of delay of 12 and a size of 6. Item B has a cost of delay of 9 and a size of 3. Using WSJF, which goes first?
options: Item B, with a score of 3
Item A, with a score of 2
Item A, because its cost of delay is higher
explanation: A: 12 ÷ 6 = 2. B: 9 ÷ 3 = 3. The higher WSJF score goes first, so B is done before A.
ref: Agile Practice Guide, Glossary (weighted shortest job first)

links.label: Agile Practice Guide, Glossary (weighted shortest job first)

q: In a workshop each stakeholder receives 100 points and spreads them over the items they want most. In which technique do stakeholders "spend" a fixed budget like this?
options: Stack ranking with a single owner
explanation: In buy-a-feature or the $100 test, stakeholders spend a budget on items. It surfaces true preferences.

q: What is the main purpose of a minimum viable product (MVP)?
options: To learn: to test assumptions and get feedback from real users with the smallest version possible
explanation: Focused on learning, the MVP is the smallest version of a product that allows a team to validate assumptions and gain feedback from real users.
ref: Agile Practice Guide, Glossary (minimum viable product)

links.label: Agile Practice Guide, Glossary (minimum viable product)

q: After early experiments a team knows what customers want. It now plans the smallest version with enough features to be offered to the market and deliver value. Which term describes it?
explanation: The MMP is focused on release: the smallest version of a product with enough features to be offered to the market.
ref: Agile Practice Guide, Glossary (minimum marketable product)

links.label: Agile Practice Guide, Glossary (minimum marketable product)

q: What is a minimum business increment (MBI)?
options: The smallest deliverable piece of functionality that has value to the business
The smallest team that can do the work without help from any other departments
The first sprint of a project
explanation: The MBI is the smallest deliverable piece of functionality that has value to the business, helping the organization realize that value quickly.
ref: Agile Practice Guide, Glossary (minimum business increment)

links.label: Agile Practice Guide, Glossary (minimum business increment)

q: Why does frequent delivery of small increments reduce risk?
options: Because small increments need no testing
Because the customer cannot change their mind
Because wrong requirements and integration problems are found early, when they are cheap to fix
explanation: Frequent delivery limits the cost of getting requirements wrong and reveals integration or environment issues early.

q: What confirms that an increment is actually valuable?
options: A status report saying it is complete
Releasing it, so customers and stakeholders can judge whether the outcome is worth the investment
The number of story points it had
explanation: Only a released increment allows customers and stakeholders to decide whether the outcome is worth the investment.

q: As a general guideline, how often should a team demonstrate working product?
options: Once at the end of the project
At least once every two weeks
explanation: As a general guideline, demonstrate whatever the team has as a working product at least once every two weeks, which is frequent enough to prevent heading in the wrong direction.

q: A senior stakeholder wants to know how the agile project is progressing. What is the best response?
options: Invite them to the next demonstration and show them the team's information radiator
Tell them to wait until the project ends
Ask the team to stop work for a full week and prepare a slide deck for the stakeholders
explanation: Agile teams show progress through working product in demonstrations and keep status visible on information radiators, instead of producing lengthy reports.

q: An increment meets the definition of done on Wednesday. Marketing wants it out today; the team would prefer next week. Who decides whether and when it is released?
explanation: Once the definition of done is met the increment can be released. The product owner decides which release option balances customer benefit, risk and overhead.

q: What is technical debt?
options: Money owed to a software supplier
The deferred cost of work not done at an earlier point in the product's life
The cost of the team's equipment
The budget overrun reported to the sponsor at the very end of a software project
explanation: Technical debt is the deferred cost of work not done earlier, such as shortcuts and missing tests. It makes later changes slower and is reduced by refactoring.

q: To meet a deadline, a manager tells the team to skip automated tests for the next three sprints. What is the most likely result?
options: Permanently higher velocity in every later iteration
Growing technical debt that slows later work
explanation: Skipping quality work defers its cost. The debt accumulates, and every later change becomes harder and slower.

q: What is continuous delivery?
options: Delivering feature increments to customers immediately, often using small batches and automation
Delivering the whole product once at the end
explanation: Continuous delivery is the practice of delivering feature increments immediately to customers, often through small batches of work and automation technology.

q: Two backlog items have similar business value. One depends on an untried technology that could derail the release. Besides business value, which factor often moves a backlog item earlier in the order?
options: It is the easiest to document
The team finds it the most enjoyable
It carries high risk or uncertainty, so doing it early gives learning sooner
explanation: High-risk items are often done early so that problems surface while there is still time and budget to respond. Dependencies and effort also influence the order.
ref: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, 7.7.2.5; Agile Practice Guide, 5.2.1

q: How does agile stakeholder engagement differ from a predictive approach?
options: Stakeholders are excluded until the end
Stakeholders are involved continuously and give feedback on working product every iteration
explanation: Agile projects require continuous feedback on features and user stories to keep the product aligned with stakeholder needs.

q: Which prioritization technique produces a single ordered list with no ties?
explanation: Stack ranking gives one ordered list with no ties. It is clarifying, sparks debate and needs a single decision owner.
